opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is closer than many people assume, but it's not a simple matter of "plug a language model into a robot and you're done."

Large language models gave us something very important: a demonstration that if you scale up data and compute on a general objective, you get capabilities that look like understanding, reasoning, and common sense. That's a huge gift to embodied intelligence. A robot needs to know that a cup can hold water, that you shouldn't put a phone in the microwave, that "tidy the table" implies a whole sequence of sub-goals. Language models already carry much of that world knowledge, so it makes sense to build on top of them rather than start from zero.

But language is a compressed, human-curated description of the world. It's very good at the "what" and the "why," and much weaker at the "how": the continuous, physical, millisecond-level details of how much force to apply, how an object deforms, what happens when something slips. You can't easily read those things off text. So embodied intelligence has to develop its own models that are grounded in vision, in 3D, in physics, and ultimately in action.

The way I see it, there are roughly three layers. At the top is high-level semantic understanding and planning, where language models are already very useful. In the middle is a model of the world, something that can predict how the scene will change if I do something. That's where I think a lot of the real work is, and it connects closely to video generation and world models. At the bottom is control, turning intentions into actual motor commands. The field is still figuring out whether these should be one unified model or a stack of specialized ones.

My intuition is that, in the long run, embodied intelligence won't just be a downstream application of language models. It may feed back into them. A model that has learned from interacting with the physical world, that has seen cause and effect rather than just read about it, could end up with a more robust kind of understanding. So right now embodied AI borrows heavily from LLMs, but I'd expect the relationship to become two-way.

The biggest gap is data. Language models had the whole internet. Embodied intelligence doesn't have an equivalent yet; robot data is expensive, slow to collect, and very heterogeneous. That's why I'm optimistic about approaches that use generative models, like simulation or video, to scale up experience. Whoever solves the data problem will probably define what the "foundation model" for embodied intelligence actually looks like.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest way to say it is that embodied intelligence has been living in the shadow of large language models, and that's both a gift and a trap.

The gift is obvious. Language models gave us a working recipe: scale the data, scale the model, let a general representation emerge instead of hand-designing one. Before that, robotics was a thousand small problems solved a thousand small ways. You tuned one controller for one gripper on one table. The LLM era told everyone, maybe this can be one problem. And the multimodal pieces, the vision-language models especially, gave us something very practical: a brain that already understands what a kitchen is, what a cup is, what "put it on the left" means. You don't have to teach that from scratch anymore. So a lot of the early embodied work is essentially borrowing that brain and bolting on an action head. That's where the vision-language-action models come from.

The trap is that people assume the recipe transfers one to one, and it doesn't. Language has this incredibly convenient property: the internet is a free, enormous, already-labeled dataset, and the output is in the same space as the input. Tokens in, tokens out. Robotics has none of that. The data doesn't exist until you collect it, collecting it costs real money and real time, and the output is a continuous motion in a physical world with contact, friction, latency, and consequences. A wrong token in a chat is an awkward sentence. A wrong action is a dropped glass or a broken arm. So you can't just say "we'll scale" and wait. You have to decide what to scale.

That's why I think the field is, as you say, developing its own models rather than just inheriting them. And I'd frame the split this way. The language model is very good at the slow, semantic layer: understanding the task, decomposing it, reasoning about what should happen. It's a poor fit for the fast layer: the millisecond-level control, the physical intuition of how an object will move when you push it. Those are different kinds of knowledge. One is about meaning, the other is about dynamics. So the architectures that are emerging tend to have some separation, a slower system that reasons and a faster system that acts, with the interesting question being how tightly they're coupled and whether they're trained jointly.

The other thing that's genuinely new is the role of world models and generative video. If language models learned from text that humans wrote, embodied models may end up learning a lot from video, real and synthetic, because that's where physics lives. Predicting what the world looks like a second from now is a very different pretraining objective than predicting the next word, and I think it's closer to what a body actually needs. Simulation and generated data become a way to pay for the data that reality won't give you cheaply.

So my view is that the relationship is going to look less like "embodied AI is an application of LLMs" and more like two siblings with a shared parent. They share the philosophy of general models, large pretraining, and emergence. But the embodied one has to grow its own organs for perception-to-action, for physical priors, for safety, for learning from relatively little data. And honestly, I suspect the influence will eventually run the other way too. A model that has to be right about the physical world is being held to a stricter standard of grounding than a model that only has to sound right. That discipline may teach the language side something.

r003.rationale: The response describes separate reasoning and acting systems while leaving open how tightly they are coupled; it does not suggest interaction only through an interface layer.

r004.rationale: It emphasizes physical control and embodied models’ own needs, but does not argue that short-term priority should be task execution over integrating a language system.

astra-6.text:
I see large language models as an important foundation for embodied intelligence, but not the whole solution. Language gives us a powerful way to represent knowledge, interpret instructions, and reason about tasks. An embodied system also has to perceive its surroundings, take actions, and learn from what happens. That interaction with the physical world introduces challenges that language alone cannot resolve.

So, as embodied intelligence develops its own models, I think the question is how to connect those capabilities. A model might understand what “pick up the cup carefully” means, but it still needs to determine how to grasp that particular cup and adjust if it slips. Planning and physical execution have to work together.

I would expect the relationship to be complementary. Embodied intelligence can build on the capabilities of language models while developing models and training methods grounded in perception, action, and feedback. Over time, that experience could also help models develop a richer understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response says language models are an important foundation and that language alone cannot resolve physical-world challenges; it does not state that embodied task performance depends little on language understanding.

r002.rationale: It says language models can interpret instructions and embodied systems must act, but does not identify translating instructions into action sequences as a role for large language models.

r003.rationale: The response describes complementary capabilities but does not suggest they interact only through an interface layer.

r004.rationale: It does not prioritize task execution over language-system integration in the short term; it describes the relationship as complementary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think large language models provide a very important foundation, but embodied intelligence has to go beyond language. An embodied agent needs to perceive its surroundings, take actions, and learn from the consequences. Knowing how to describe a task is different from being able to execute it reliably in the physical world.

So I don’t see this as choosing between large language models and a completely separate set of models. Language models can help with understanding instructions and planning, while embodied models need to connect that understanding to perception and control. The interesting question is how much of that can be learned in one unified model, and where specialized components are still useful.

As the field develops, I think the key will be the learning loop: act, observe what happens, and improve. Language gives us access to a great deal of human knowledge, but interaction gives us feedback that text alone cannot provide.
